1	# JusPrin product definition
2	
3	**Status:** Canonical product direction for the `jusprin-newui` production branch.
4	
5	**Source:** Consolidated from product discovery on `jusprin-v2-poc`. Historical inspection evidence remains on that branch; see [POC reference](poc-reference.md).
6	
7	## Executive summary
8	
9	An AI agent can remove much of a slicer’s technical complexity, but it cannot eliminate the need for user interaction.
10	
11	The boundary is:
12	
13	> The user tells the system what is physically true, what the object means, and what outcome is wanted. The agent chooses the technical printing strategy. The user verifies consequential decisions and remains in control of the physical machine.
14	
15	This produces three classes of OrcaSlicer features:
16	
17	1. **User-decision surfaces must remain prominent.**
18	   These capture information the agent cannot reliably obtain: physical setup, functional intent, geometry meaning, aesthetic preferences, legal restrictions, and control over real-world actions.
19	
20	2. **Shared agent-and-user surfaces should be redesigned.**
21	   The agent proposes a solution, explains it, and draws attention to uncertainty. The user reviews the result visually instead of manipulating dozens of parameters.
22	
23	3. **Implementation settings can disappear from the primary interface.**
24	   The agent can usually manage line widths, speeds, infill mechanics, cooling, retraction, support parameters, and similar technical details.
25	
26	The final product should therefore retain nine primary surfaces:
27	
28	1. Project knowledge
29	2. Physical setup
30	3. Print intent
31	4. Objects and plates
32	5. Essential geometry editing
33	6. Local meaning and overrides
34	7. Print-plan verification
35	8. Print preflight and live control
36	9. Calibration and troubleshooting
37	
38	These are not remnants of a legacy slicer. They are the information and control boundary between a person, an AI agent, and a physical manufacturing process.
39	
40	The interface should not give every retained feature equal weight. Features fall into four visibility levels:
41	
42	1. **Default** — continuously visible in an ordinary project.
43	2. **Contextual** — appears when the project, current selection, or agent uncertainty makes it relevant.
44	3. **On demand** — available through Project details, More, or the expert layer.
45	4. **Interruptive** — normally hidden, but made prominent when a consequential warning, mismatch, or unresolved decision occurs.
46	
47	Frequency alone does not determine visibility. A control can be rarely used but interruptive because overlooking it would be costly or unsafe.
48	
49	---
50	
51	# 1. Why an AI agent sometimes lacks enough information
52	
53	Before deciding which UI to retain, it helps to distinguish the different reasons an agent cannot safely make a decision.
54	
55	## 1.1 The agent cannot observe physical reality reliably
56	
57	A slicer may say that a particular nozzle, plate, or filament is selected, but that does not prove it is installed.
58	
59	Examples include:
60	
61	- The build plate was changed manually.
62	- The AMS contains a different spool than expected.
63	- Filament is wet, old, tangled, or nearly empty.
64	- A hardened nozzle was replaced with a standard nozzle.
65	- Glue was or was not applied.
66	- The print bed is occupied.
67	- A previous print remains attached to the plate.
68	
69	The agent can detect some of these conditions using printer sensors or a camera, but uncertainty must remain visible.
70	
71	## 1.2 The agent does not know what the geometry means
72	
73	A mesh contains shapes, not intentions.
74	
75	The agent may identify a hole, thin wall, flat face, or overhang, but it does not inherently know whether that feature is:
76	
77	- A precision bearing surface
78	- A screw hole
79	- A snap fit
80	- A decorative opening
81	- A sacrificial support
82	- A face that must remain smooth
83	- A surface hidden after assembly
84	- A region intended to flex
85	- A deliberately thin membrane
86	
87	This is why essential geometry editing and semantic annotation must remain.
88	
89	## 1.3 The agent does not know the user’s priorities
90	
91	There is rarely one objectively correct slicing strategy. A user may prioritize:
92	
93	- Appearance
94	- Strength
95	- Dimensional accuracy
96	- Speed
97	- Material savings
98	- Heat resistance
99	- Flexibility
100	- Watertightness
101	- Minimal support marks
102	- A particular color arrangement
103	
104	These priorities can conflict. The agent needs the user to define what “good” means.
105	
106	## 1.4 Some decisions are subjective
107	
108	Seam placement, surface texture, layer visibility, support scars, color boundaries, and acceptable print time are personal judgments.
109	
110	An agent can recommend an option, but it cannot determine the user’s taste from the model alone.
111	
112	## 1.5 Some actions have consequential real-world effects
113	
114	Starting a print consumes material, occupies a machine, creates heat and motion, and may run unattended for hours. Firmware updates and calibration changes can alter the behavior of the printer.
115	
116	The agent can prepare these actions, but the user needs final authority over them.
117	
118	## 1.6 Some information concerns ownership, law, or safety
119	
120	The agent cannot invent or silently change:
121	
122	- Authorship
123	- Licensing
124	- Commercial-use permission
125	- Safety warnings
126	- Assembly instructions
127	- Bill-of-materials information
128	- Intended use
129	- Privacy and cloud-connectivity preferences
130	
131	These are authoritative project facts, not slicing parameters.
132	
133	---
134	
135	# 2. The surfaces that must remain
136	
137	## 2.0 Project-window hierarchy
138	
139	The Project window should not treat Prepare, Preview, and Info as three equal destinations.
140	
141	- **Prepare is the dominant, persistent workspace.** It is where users inspect the model, communicate intent, manipulate geometry, resolve uncertainty, and review the agent's plan.
142	- **Check print opens Orca Preview in a modal window.** Prepare remains underneath; closing Check returns focus to Prepare. It is a secondary action when the active plate has a valid slice.
143	- **Info becomes Project details.** It is a drawer opened from the project name or menu. The agent reads its contents continuously even when the drawer is closed.
144	- **Print opens Send preflight.** It never sends directly. Explicit Send remains the consequential commitment.
145	
146	The normal flow is:
147	
148	`Prepare -> Check print -> return to Prepare if correction is needed -> Print -> Send preflight -> explicit Send`
149	
150	### Default Project-window composition
151	
152	The default window should contain:
153	
154	- Project name and saved/unsaved state
155	- Compact printer pointer: target printer, nozzle, build plate, and material
156	- Compact, editable intent summary
157	- Compact active plate/object summary
158	- 3D Prepare canvas
159	- Essential direct-manipulation tools
160	- Compact pinned agent plan
161	- Highest unresolved assumption, compromise, or risk
162	- Check print
163	- Print
164	- Consequential warnings when applicable
165	
166	The canvas is the primary human-agent collaboration surface. It must make the build plate and model visible, support camera rotation, pan, zoom, selection, and direct spatial manipulation, and show the changes the agent makes.
167	
168	The compact summaries should keep the governing assumptions visible without expanding full editors. Examples:
169	
170	> Decorative · appearance first · protect front surface · under 5 hours
171	
172	> Plate 1 · Fuzzy Heart · 1 copy · PLA Matte
173	
174	A one-object project should not permanently display a large object tree. A complete intent questionnaire should not remain expanded after it has been answered.
175	
176	### Direct resolution of uncertainty
177	
178	Warnings should link to the user action that resolves them rather than expecting the user to translate them into legacy slicer controls:
179	
180	- `Support enters this hole` -> `Protect this opening`
181	- `Seam crosses a visible face` -> `Mark visible face`
182	- `Strength direction is unclear` -> `Show load direction`
183	- `Part may not fit` -> `Enter critical dimension`
184	- `Support may be hard to remove` -> `Adjust supports`
185	
186	Each feature still has one authoritative home, but summaries, warnings, and resolution actions may appear elsewhere. For example, Printer Configuration owns the installed hardware state while Prepare shows a compact pointer and any mismatch.
187	
188	## 2.1 Project knowledge
189	
190	This surface answers: **What is this project, and what does someone need to know about it?**
191	
192	OrcaSlicer exposes model descriptions, creator information, pictures, license information, profile notes, accessories, bills of materials, assembly guides, and other attachments.
193	
194	A project inspected during product discovery contained a safety instruction limiting it to electric tea lights. That information could affect how the agent evaluates material, temperature exposure, and intended use.
195	
196	### Why the agent cannot decide this alone
197	
198	The mesh does not contain reliable authorship, licensing, safety, assembly, or use-case information. An agent may extract clues, but it must not treat guesses as project facts.
199	
200	### What should remain
201	
202	- Project name and saved/unsaved state
203	- Project description
204	- Author and license
205	- Safety and usage instructions
206	- Reference pictures
207	- Assembly instructions
208	- Bill of materials and accessories
209	- Important profile notes
210	- Project save, version, backup, and ownership controls
211	
212	### What the agent should do
213	
214	The agent should read this material before planning the print, highlight contradictions, and ask about missing safety or assembly information when relevant.
215	
216	Only the project name and saved/unsaved state need to remain in the normal Project-window chrome. The rest belongs in the Project details drawer and surfaces automatically only when consequential:
217	
218	- Safety or usage warning: on import, when it affects planning, and before Print
219	- License restriction: when sharing, publishing, using commercially, or exporting
220	- Assembly instructions: for multi-part projects and plate organization
221	- Bill of materials or accessories: when non-printed components are required
222	- Reference image: when it clarifies orientation, color, or intended appearance
223	- Profile note: when the agent proposes deviating from it
224	- Recovery or version warning: when work is unsaved or versions conflict
225	
226	The user should not have to open Project details for its contents to influence the plan.
227	
228	---
229	
230	## 2.2 Physical printer setup
231	
232	This surface answers: **What hardware and material will actually perform the print?**
233	
234	### What should remain
235	
236	- Target printer
237	- Nozzle diameter and nozzle type
238	- Build-plate type
239	- Loaded filament and material
240	- Filament color
241	- AMS or multi-material slot mapping
242	- Printer availability and current condition
243	- Important mismatches between configuration and observed hardware
244	
245	### Why the agent cannot decide this alone
246	
247	Configured state and physical state can diverge. Selecting “PLA” in software does not establish that PLA is actually loaded, dry, correctly mapped, or compatible with the installed plate and nozzle.
248	
249	### What the agent should do
250	
251	- Discover printers and materials automatically
252	- Read AMS and printer state where available
253	- Compare observed state with the project
254	- Recommend compatible profiles
255	- Explain mismatches
256	- Ask the user only about unresolved physical facts
257	
258	The existing setup wizard’s enormous lists of printer and filament profiles should become hardware discovery followed by a short confirmation.
259	
260	---
261	
262	## 2.3 Print intent
263	
264	This surface answers: **What outcome does the user want?**
265	
266	Instead of beginning with hundreds of process parameters, the product should ask for meaningful requirements.
267	
268	### What should remain
269	
270	- Intended use
271	- Visual versus functional priority
272	- Strength direction
273	- Accuracy requirements
274	- Important dimensions or clearances
275	- Heat, chemical, outdoor, food-contact, or flexibility requirements
276	- Desired surface quality
277	- Maximum acceptable print time
278	- Material or color requirements
279	- Acceptable and unacceptable support contact
280	- Whether this is a prototype or final part
281	
282	### Why the agent cannot decide this alone
283	
284	The same model can legitimately be printed with different orientations, materials, wall structures, infill, supports, and tolerances depending on its purpose.
285	
286	A decorative prototype and a load-bearing final component may use identical geometry but require completely different plans.
287	
288	### What the agent should do
289	
290	Translate intent into technical settings. For example:
291	
292	> “This is a visible decorative object, so I oriented it to protect the front surface, moved the seam to the rear, and accepted a longer print to reduce visible layer artifacts.”
293	
294	The user should judge that reasoning without having to configure every underlying value.
295	
296	The full intent editor should appear during project creation, import, or when requirements are incomplete. Afterward, Prepare should retain only a compact editable summary. Specialized questions such as food contact, flexibility, critical clearances, and protected support surfaces should appear contextually rather than in every project.
297	
298	---
299	
300	## 2.4 Objects, parts, and plates
301	
302	This surface answers: **What exactly is included in this job?**
303	
304	OrcaSlicer’s object and plate tree is essential, although its presentation can be simplified.
305	
306	### What should remain
307	
308	- Every plate in the project
309	- Every object and part
310	- Object names
311	- Quantity and duplicates
312	- Which objects are enabled
313	- Which material or extruder each object uses
314	- Modifiers, support enforcers, and support blockers
315	- Object-specific requirements
316	- Print order where it matters
317	- Search for complex projects
318	
319	### Why the agent cannot decide this alone
320	
321	The agent cannot assume that every imported object should be printed or that apparently duplicated parts are accidental. A modifier may encode engineering intent that is invisible in the rendered outer surface.
322	
323	Multi-plate organization can also represent batches, material differences, alternative versions, or assembly groups.
324	
325	### What the agent should do
326	
327	Arrange objects, detect accidental overlaps, identify likely duplicates, balance plates, and suggest grouping—but show the resulting job manifest for confirmation.
328	
329	For a simple one-object, one-material, one-plate project, show a compact job summary by default. Expand the full object-and-part tree contextually when the project contains multiple objects, parts, plates, materials, modifiers, or print-order constraints. Search should appear only when the project is complex enough to need it.
330	
331	---
332	
333	## 2.5 Essential geometry editing
334	
335	This surface answers: **Does the printable geometry need to be intentionally changed?**
336	
337	This was underrepresented in the previous report. Geometry editing must remain a first-class capability.
338	
339	### Default operations
340	
341	- Add and remove models
342	- Select parts
343	- Move, rotate, and scale
344	- Place a model on a chosen face
345	- Arrange models on the plate
346	- Duplicate and change quantity
347	- Undo and redo
348	
349	### Contextual operations
350	
351	These remain first-class capabilities but should appear under More, through the selected-object menu, or when the situation calls for them:
352	
353	- Mirror
354	- Cut and split
355	- Merge or assemble related parts
356	- Add text or labels
357	- Measure dimensions and clearances
358	- Work with multiple plates
359	- Repair or identify problematic geometry
360	- Create intentional modifiers
361	- Paint supports, seams, materials, or other region-specific behavior
362	
363	Examples of contextual surfacing include offering Cut for an oversized model, Measure when fit or clearance matters, Repair when mesh defects are detected, and region annotation when the agent cannot determine where support contact is acceptable.
364	
365	### Why the agent cannot decide this alone
366	
367	Changing geometry can change the object’s meaning.
368	
369	The agent cannot safely assume that it may:
370	
371	- Cut a model into pieces
372	- Fill or enlarge a hole
373	- Change scale
374	- Move two components relative to one another
375	- Mirror an asymmetric part
376	- Emboss text
377	- Remove an apparently unnecessary detail
378	- Reorient an assembly
379	- Create a different mating surface
380	
381	Even when a change improves printability, it may make the part unusable.
382	
383	### What the agent should do
384	
385	The agent may propose geometry changes and generate previews:
386	
387	> “Splitting the model here eliminates most supports and hides the joint on the rear surface.”
388	
389	But the user should review meaning-changing operations. Direct manipulation must remain available because communicating spatial corrections in words is often slower than moving or painting them on the model.
390	
391	---
392	
393	## 2.6 Local meaning and region-level overrides
394	
395	This surface answers: **Are different parts or surfaces subject to different requirements?**
396	
397	Global instructions such as “make it strong” are often insufficient.
398	
399	### What should remain
400	
401	Users need ways to identify:
402	
403	- Faces that must remain smooth
404	- Surfaces where support contact is allowed or forbidden
405	- Precision holes and mating surfaces
406	- Areas requiring additional strength
407	- Flexible or sacrificial regions
408	- Visible versus hidden faces
409	- Preferred or forbidden seam locations
410	- Different material or color regions
411	- Areas where texture is intentional
412	- Object-specific print requirements
413	
414	### Why the agent cannot decide this alone
415	
416	Computer vision can estimate geometry, but it cannot reliably know the functional role of every region.
417	
418	For example, an agent may place a seam on the geometrically least visible face, unaware that the face mates with another part. It may strengthen the thickest region even though failure occurs around a small mounting hole.
419	
420	### What the agent should do
421	
422	Use semantic labels to generate modifiers and technical settings automatically. Users should describe meaning; they should not normally need to configure local speeds, wall counts, or infill percentages themselves.
423	
424	---
425	
426	## 2.7 Agent print plan
427	
428	This surface answers: **What strategy has the agent chosen, and why?**
429	
430	This is the AI-first replacement for most of OrcaSlicer’s process-setting panels.
431	
432	### What should be shown by default
433	
434	- Selected orientation
435	- Overall material, strength, support, and surface-quality strategy
436	- Most important assumption the agent could not verify
437	- Most important compromise or unresolved risk
438	
439	### What should appear when expanded
440	
441	- Detailed rationale and alternative plans
442	- Confidence by decision
443	- Important deviations from the normal printer profile
444	- Full change history
445	- Numerical implementation settings through the expert layer
446	
447	### Why this surface is needed
448	
449	Even when the agent has enough information to choose technical values, hiding its entire plan would make errors difficult to recognize.
450	
451	The user may not need to know that a particular wall speed is 72 mm/s, but they should know that the plan emphasizes surface quality over speed.
452	
453	### What the agent can normally control
454	
455	- Layer-height strategy
456	- Line widths
457	- Wall and top/bottom structure
458	- Infill density and pattern
459	- Speeds and acceleration
460	- Cooling and temperature within qualified ranges
461	- Retraction and wiping
462	- Bridge behavior
463	- Support style, density, and interface parameters
464	- Brim, skirt, priming, and adhesion aids
465	- Purging and flushing calculations
466	- Seam implementation after the user states the preferred region
467	- Printer-specific G-code from a trusted profile
468	
469	These settings should remain accessible to experts, but they do not need to be primary beginner-facing surfaces.
470	
471	Do not always show time and material estimates in Prepare. Show them there only after a valid background slice exists. Until then, the plan can say `Ready to check`.
472	
473	---
474	
475	## 2.8 Check print: print-plan verification
476	
477	This surface answers: **What will the printer actually do?**
478	
479	OrcaSlicer’s Preview capability is not merely an expert visualization. It is the last opportunity to discover a bad plan before material and machine time are consumed. **Check print** opens the current valid slice in a modal window using Orca's real Preview widget and G-code renderer. The window closes if that slice or its project changes. For now, Print stays the primary action for every valid slice and Check print stays in its menu; agent findings do not change that action.
480	
481	### Default verification
482	
483	- Overall appearance of the sliced result
484	- Estimated time
485	- Material usage and cost
486	- Highest-priority warnings
487	- Comparison with the user’s stated intent
488	
489	When supports exist, support verification becomes the default Check view:
490	
491	- Support locations
492	- Contact surfaces and likely scars
493	- Supports that may be difficult to remove
494	- Supports entering holes, cavities, or mating regions
495	- A direct Adjust supports or Mark protected areas action that returns to Prepare
496	
497	If no supports exist, Check should emphasize the most consequential detected risk instead.
498	
499	### Contextual verification
500	
501	- Seams on protected or visible surfaces
502	- Risky bridges and overhangs
503	- Thin or missing features
504	- First-layer contact problems
505	- Unsupported islands
506	- Unexpected gaps or collisions
507	- Material or color changes
508	- Purge volume and waste
509	- Prime tower and extruder assignments
510	
511	### Expert verification
512	
513	OrcaSlicer’s more detailed views should remain available on demand:
514	
515	- Line type
516	- Layer height
517	- Line width
518	- Speed
519	- Fan speed
520	- Temperature
521	- Volumetric flow
522	- Layer time
523	- Extruder assignment
524	- Layer-by-layer playback
525	- Individual toolpath playback
526	- Visibility toggles for walls, infill, bridges, supports, travel, retraction, wiping, and seams
527	- Raw G-code inspection
528	
529	### Why the agent cannot independently verify its own plan
530	
531	The preview is produced from the same assumptions and algorithms that created the plan. It is evidence, but it is not independent knowledge of the user’s intent.
532	
533	An agent may verify that a toolpath is internally consistent while still misunderstanding which surface must remain smooth or which opening must stay unobstructed.
534	
535	### What the agent should do
536	
537	Inspect the complete preview automatically and present a short risk-focused report. The user should review the meaningful consequences instead of manually examining every toolpath by default.
538	
539	Layer count and the complete extrusion-role legend are not beginner decision aids. Keep them in Inspect toolpaths with the other expert diagnostics.
540	
541	---
542	
543	## 2.9 Print preflight
544	
545	This surface answers: **Is the correct job about to be sent to the correct physical machine?**
546	
547	Prepare should contain a visible Print entry point. Print opens this preflight; it does not bypass it:
548	
549	`Print -> Send preflight -> explicit Send`
550	
551	The current Print action opens Orca's existing Select Machine or printer-host send dialog, which requires a separate send/upload choice. The complete JusPrin preflight checklist below remains future product work.
552	
553	### What should remain
554	
555	- Job name and thumbnail
556	- Destination printer
557	- Selected plate
558	- Time and material estimate
559	- Filament and AMS mapping
560	- Plate-type confirmation
561	- Bed-leveling choice
562	- Flow-calibration choice
563	- Timelapse choice
564	- First-layer inspection
565	- Build-plate detection
566	- Tangle and clumping detection
567	- AI-monitoring behavior and sensitivity
568	- Recovery options
569	- Warnings about disabled checks
570	- Explicit Send control
571	
572	### Why the agent cannot decide this alone
573	
574	This is where digital assumptions become a real physical operation. The chosen printer may be occupied, prepared with another plate, located remotely, or loaded with valuable material.
575	
576	Some monitoring options also involve privacy, camera use, false-positive tolerance, or printer-specific limitations.
577	
578	### What the agent should do
579	
580	Perform the preflight, recommend safe defaults, and block obviously inconsistent jobs. The user should see a concise checklist and authorize sending.
581	
582	---
583	
584	## 2.10 Live printing and device control
585	
586	This surface answers: **What is happening now, and can the user intervene?**
587	
588	OrcaSlicer’s Device surface demonstrates that an AI slicer is also partly a printer-control product.
589	
590	### What should remain immediately accessible
591	
592	- Camera
593	- Job progress
594	- Current layer and remaining time
595	- Printer state
596	- Nozzle and bed temperatures
597	- Important fan or light controls
598	- Health and fault alerts
599	- Pause
600	- Resume
601	- Stop
602	
603	Manual movement, homing, detailed fan control, storage, and file management can be contextual or expert functions.
604	
605	### Why the agent cannot control this invisibly
606	
607	Sensors and vision systems can be wrong. Users may notice a sound, smell, obstruction, detaching part, or safety concern that the system cannot observe.
608	
609	Pause and stop are human override mechanisms. They should never be hidden inside a conversation or require the agent’s cooperation.
610	
611	### What the agent should do
612	
613	Monitor the job, explain anomalies, recommend intervention, and automatically pause only under rules the user has authorized in advance. It should clearly report why an automatic intervention occurred.
614	
615	---
616	
617	## 2.11 Calibration and troubleshooting
618	
619	This surface answers: **Is the printer-material combination behaving as expected?**
620	
621	The audit found both guided calibration pages and more advanced generators.
622	
623	### Relevant calibration capabilities
624	
625	- Flow dynamics
626	- Flow rate
627	- Temperature
628	- Pressure advance
629	- Retraction
630	- Maximum volumetric speed
631	- VFA
632	- Junction deviation
633	- Input-shaping frequency and damping
634	
635	### Why the agent cannot completely own calibration
636	
637	Calibration depends on physical evidence:
638	
639	- Filament may be wet.
640	- Adhesion may be poor.
641	- Transparent or reflective filament may confuse optical sensors.
642	- A nozzle may be worn or partially obstructed.
643	- A user may judge two samples differently.
644	- Automatic measurements contain uncertainty.
645	- An apparently better surface may reduce strength or accuracy elsewhere.
646	
647	### What the agent should do
648	
649	The agent should:
650	
651	1. Diagnose the observed symptom.
652	2. Decide whether calibration is justified.
653	3. Select the appropriate test.
654	4. Choose safe test ranges.
655	5. Explain what to observe.
656	6. Analyze sensor data or photographs.
657	7. Recommend a result.
658	8. Ask the user to confirm before updating a persistent printer or filament profile.
659	
660	The user should not be presented with every calibration parameter unless manual control is requested.
661	
662	---
663	
664	## 2.12 Privacy, updates, portability, and expert administration
665	
666	These functions are used less frequently, but they are important for particular users and organizations.
667	
668	### User-owned decisions
669	
670	- Cloud login region
671	- Stealth or offline mode
672	- Network-plugin use
673	- Preset synchronization
674	- Multi-device management
675	- Firmware and application update timing
676	- Camera and monitoring privacy
677	- Backup and recovery policy
678	- Importing and replacing configurations
679	- Ownership and export of project data
680	
681	### Capabilities that should remain available
682	
683	- Import 3MF, STL, STEP, SVG, OBJ, AMF, ZIP archives, and configurations
684	- Export models, projects, sliced plates, G-code, and preset bundles
685	- Export printer, filament, and process profiles
686	- Manage downloaded and stored printer files
687	- Access timelapses
688	- Run network diagnostics
689	- Open configuration data
690	- Enable developer tools
691	
692	### Why the agent cannot decide these alone
693	
694	These choices affect privacy, compatibility, organizational policy, intellectual property, and the user’s ability to leave the product.
695	
696	The agent can simplify the workflows, but it should not silently enable cloud communication, install firmware, replace profiles, or trap projects in a proprietary format.
697	
698	---
699	
700	# 3. Recommended final product structure
701	
702	The application should use one main window rather than turning every stage of a print into equal global navigation.
703	
704	## 3.1 Home
705	
706	Home is the hub for:
707	
708	- Printer cards showing availability, condition, and loaded filament
709	- Project gallery, open, and project status
710	- Import of 3MF, STL, STEP, SVG, OBJ, AMF, and ZIP files
711	- Entry to project versions and backups
712	- Launching Monitor
713	
714	## 3.2 Project window
715	
716	The Project window contains the print-planning lifecycle without dividing it into equal destinations:
717	
718	- **Prepare:** dominant workspace containing intent, objects and plates, the 3D canvas, geometry editing, local meaning, and the agent plan
719	- **Check print:** temporary sliced-verification mode
720	- **Project details:** drawer for authoritative project knowledge
721	- **Print:** entry point to Send preflight
722	
723	Prepare may point to Printer Configuration, but it does not own machine calibration, filament inventory, maintenance, or privacy settings.
724	
725	## 3.3 Printer Configuration
726	
727	Printer Configuration owns:
728	
729	- Target printer, nozzle, and build-plate configuration
730	- Loaded filament, material colors, AMS, and multi-material inventory
731	- Calibration workflows
732	- Troubleshooting and maintenance
733	- Firmware-update timing
734	- Camera and monitoring privacy
735	- Network plugins and diagnostic tools
736	- Stored printer files and timelapses
737	
738	Prepare displays a compact pointer to this state and surfaces mismatches; it does not duplicate the complete configuration UI.
739	
740	## 3.4 Monitor
741	
742	Monitor is a pop-out surface so it can remain visible while the user works elsewhere. It owns:
743	
744	- Camera
745	- Progress, current layer, and remaining time
746	- Printer state
747	- Nozzle and bed temperatures
748	- Health and fault alerts
749	- Pause, Resume, and Stop as never-hidden human overrides
750	
751	Manual movement, homing, detailed fan or light control, storage, and file management are contextual.
752	
753	## 3.5 Overlays and application-level layers
754	
755	- **Send preflight:** final job, destination, material mapping, safety, and monitoring confirmation followed by explicit Send
756	- **Expert layer:** raw process settings, numeric per-object and per-region overrides, manual calibration ranges, toolpath diagnostics, and G-code
757	- **Preferences:** cloud region, stealth/offline behavior, network plugins, sync, updates, privacy, backup and recovery, import/export administration, and developer tools
758	
759	This structure preserves the lifecycle of a print without turning Setup, Intent, Plan, Verify, Print, Monitor, and Diagnose into nine equal screens.
760	
761	---
762	
763	# 4. Visibility hierarchy
764	
765	## 4.1 Default
766	
767	Continuously visible in the ordinary Project window:
768	
769	- Project name and saved/unsaved state
770	- Current printer, nozzle, plate, and material summary
771	- Compact intent summary
772	- Compact active plate and object summary
773	- 3D Prepare canvas
774	- Add, remove, select, move, rotate, scale, place on face, arrange, duplicate, Undo, and Redo
775	- Compact agent plan
776	- Highest unresolved assumption or risk
777	- Check print and Print
778	
779	Inside Check, the default changes to sliced appearance, time, material, cost, the highest-priority warning, and comparison with intent. When supports exist, support placement and removal risk become the default Check emphasis.
780	
781	## 4.2 Contextual
782	
783	Shown when the project or current task makes it relevant:
784	
785	- Full object, part, and plate tree
786	- Per-object material or extruder
787	- Modifiers, support enforcers, blockers, print order, and search
788	- Local surface annotations and object-specific requirements
789	- Mirror, cut, split, merge, assemble, text, measure, repair, positive/negative parts, and multi-plate distribution
790	- Seam, bridge, overhang, thin-feature, first-layer, island, and collision inspection
791	- Material changes, purge waste, prime tower, and extruder assignments
792	- Time and material estimate in Prepare after a valid background slice exists
793	- Assembly instructions, accessories, and reference pictures
794	- Calibration and maintenance recommendations
795	- Firmware updates, storage, timelapses, and multi-device management
796	
797	## 4.3 On demand
798	
799	Available through Project details, More, or the expert layer:
800	
801	- Full intent questionnaire after it has been completed
802	- Project description, author, license, pictures, BOM, assembly guide, and profile notes
803	- Version, backup, ownership, and export administration
804	- Detailed agent rationale, alternatives, confidence, profile deviations, and change history
805	- Individual speeds and accelerations
806	- Exact line widths
807	- Infill and support implementation parameters
808	- Retraction, wiping, cooling, and purge details
809	- Complete toolpath legend and playback
810	- Raw G-code
811	- Manual calibration ranges
812	- Network tests, configuration folders, developer mode, and visualization preferences
813	
814	## 4.4 Interruptive
815	
816	Normally hidden, but presented prominently at the point where the user can resolve it:
817	
818	- Wrong printer, nozzle, plate, or filament
819	- Safety or usage instruction relevant to the current plan
820	- Unsupported, missing, or defective geometry
821	- Support entering a protected region
822	- Violated dimensional requirement
823	- Material incompatible with the stated use
824	- Agent uncertainty about a meaning-changing geometry operation
825	- License conflict during sharing, publishing, commercial use, or export
826	- Unsaved work, recovery issue, or version conflict
827	- Printer-health or safety alert
828	
829	---
830	
831	# 5. The final design rule
832	
833	For every OrcaSlicer control, ask four questions:
834	
835	1. **Does this require physical information the software may not possess?**
836	   Keep a user confirmation surface.
837	
838	2. **Does this depend on the object’s purpose, meaning, or the user’s taste?**
839	   Keep an intent, annotation, or direct-editing surface.
840	
841	3. **Does this authorize a consequential, legal, private, or physical action?**
842	   Keep explicit user control.
843	
844	4. **Is this merely a technical method for achieving an already-understood goal?**
845	   Let the agent manage it and expose it only when explanation or expert control is needed.
846	
847	That rule preserves the genuinely human parts of OrcaSlicer while allowing the agent to remove most of its parameter complexity.
848

# JusPrin product definition

**Status:** Canonical product direction for the `jusprin-newui` production branch.

**Source:** Consolidated from product discovery on `jusprin-v2-poc`. Historical inspection evidence remains on that branch; see [POC reference](poc-reference.md).

## Executive summary

An AI agent can remove much of a slicer’s technical complexity, but it cannot eliminate the need for user interaction.

The boundary is:

> The user tells the system what is physically true, what the object means, and what outcome is wanted. The agent chooses the technical printing strategy. The user verifies consequential decisions and remains in control of the physical machine.

This produces three classes of OrcaSlicer features:

1. **User-decision surfaces must remain prominent.**
   These capture information the agent cannot reliably obtain: physical setup, functional intent, geometry meaning, aesthetic preferences, legal restrictions, and control over real-world actions.

2. **Shared agent-and-user surfaces should be redesigned.**
   The agent proposes a solution, explains it, and draws attention to uncertainty. The user reviews the result visually instead of manipulating dozens of parameters.

3. **Implementation settings can disappear from the primary interface.**
   The agent can usually manage line widths, speeds, infill mechanics, cooling, retraction, support parameters, and similar technical details.

The final product should therefore retain nine primary surfaces:

1. Project knowledge
2. Physical setup
3. Print intent
4. Objects and plates
5. Essential geometry editing
6. Local meaning and overrides
7. Print-plan verification
8. Print preflight and live control
9. Calibration and troubleshooting

These are not remnants of a legacy slicer. They are the information and control boundary between a person, an AI agent, and a physical manufacturing process.

The interface should not give every retained feature equal weight. Features fall into four visibility levels:

1. **Default** — continuously visible in an ordinary project.
2. **Contextual** — appears when the project, current selection, or agent uncertainty makes it relevant.
3. **On demand** — available through Project details, More, or the expert layer.
4. **Interruptive** — normally hidden, but made prominent when a consequential warning, mismatch, or unresolved decision occurs.

Frequency alone does not determine visibility. A control can be rarely used but interruptive because overlooking it would be costly or unsafe.

---

# 1. Why an AI agent sometimes lacks enough information

Before deciding which UI to retain, it helps to distinguish the different reasons an agent cannot safely make a decision.

## 1.1 The agent cannot observe physical reality reliably

A slicer may say that a particular nozzle, plate, or filament is selected, but that does not prove it is installed.

Examples include:

- The build plate was changed manually.
- The AMS contains a different spool than expected.
- Filament is wet, old, tangled, or nearly empty.
- A hardened nozzle was replaced with a standard nozzle.
- Glue was or was not applied.
- The print bed is occupied.
- A previous print remains attached to the plate.

The agent can detect some of these conditions using printer sensors or a camera, but uncertainty must remain visible.

## 1.2 The agent does not know what the geometry means

A mesh contains shapes, not intentions.

The agent may identify a hole, thin wall, flat face, or overhang, but it does not inherently know whether that feature is:

- A precision bearing surface
- A screw hole
- A snap fit
- A decorative opening
- A sacrificial support
- A face that must remain smooth
- A surface hidden after assembly
- A region intended to flex
- A deliberately thin membrane

This is why essential geometry editing and semantic annotation must remain.

## 1.3 The agent does not know the user’s priorities

There is rarely one objectively correct slicing strategy. A user may prioritize:

- Appearance
- Strength
- Dimensional accuracy
- Speed
- Material savings
- Heat resistance
- Flexibility
- Watertightness
- Minimal support marks
- A particular color arrangement

These priorities can conflict. The agent needs the user to define what “good” means.

## 1.4 Some decisions are subjective

Seam placement, surface texture, layer visibility, support scars, color boundaries, and acceptable print time are personal judgments.

An agent can recommend an option, but it cannot determine the user’s taste from the model alone.

## 1.5 Some actions have consequential real-world effects

Starting a print consumes material, occupies a machine, creates heat and motion, and may run unattended for hours. Firmware updates and calibration changes can alter the behavior of the printer.

The agent can prepare these actions, but the user needs final authority over them.

## 1.6 Some information concerns ownership, law, or safety

The agent cannot invent or silently change:

- Authorship
- Licensing
- Commercial-use permission
- Safety warnings
- Assembly instructions
- Bill-of-materials information
- Intended use
- Privacy and cloud-connectivity preferences

These are authoritative project facts, not slicing parameters.

---

# 2. The surfaces that must remain

## 2.0 Project-window hierarchy

The Project window should not treat Prepare, Preview, and Info as three equal destinations.

- **Prepare is the dominant, persistent workspace.** It is where users inspect the model, communicate intent, manipulate geometry, resolve uncertainty, and review the agent's plan.
- **Check print opens Orca Preview in a modal window.** Prepare remains underneath; closing Check returns focus to Prepare. It is a secondary action when the active plate has a valid slice.
- **Info becomes Project details.** It is a drawer opened from the project name or menu. The agent reads its contents continuously even when the drawer is closed.
- **Print opens Send preflight.** It never sends directly. Explicit Send remains the consequential commitment.

The normal flow is:

`Prepare -> Check print -> return to Prepare if correction is needed -> Print -> Send preflight -> explicit Send`

### Default Project-window composition

The default window should contain:

- Project name and saved/unsaved state
- Compact printer pointer: target printer, nozzle, build plate, and material
- Compact, editable intent summary
- Compact active plate/object summary
- 3D Prepare canvas
- Essential direct-manipulation tools
- Compact pinned agent plan
- Highest unresolved assumption, compromise, or risk
- Check print
- Print
- Consequential warnings when applicable

The canvas is the primary human-agent collaboration surface. It must make the build plate and model visible, support camera rotation, pan, zoom, selection, and direct spatial manipulation, and show the changes the agent makes.

The compact summaries should keep the governing assumptions visible without expanding full editors. Examples:

> Decorative · appearance first · protect front surface · under 5 hours

> Plate 1 · Fuzzy Heart · 1 copy · PLA Matte

A one-object project should not permanently display a large object tree. A complete intent questionnaire should not remain expanded after it has been answered.

### Direct resolution of uncertainty

Warnings should link to the user action that resolves them rather than expecting the user to translate them into legacy slicer controls:

- `Support enters this hole` -> `Protect this opening`
- `Seam crosses a visible face` -> `Mark visible face`
- `Strength direction is unclear` -> `Show load direction`
- `Part may not fit` -> `Enter critical dimension`
- `Support may be hard to remove` -> `Adjust supports`

Each feature still has one authoritative home, but summaries, warnings, and resolution actions may appear elsewhere. For example, Printer Configuration owns the installed hardware state while Prepare shows a compact pointer and any mismatch.

## 2.1 Project knowledge

This surface answers: **What is this project, and what does someone need to know about it?**

OrcaSlicer exposes model descriptions, creator information, pictures, license information, profile notes, accessories, bills of materials, assembly guides, and other attachments.

A project inspected during product discovery contained a safety instruction limiting it to electric tea lights. That information could affect how the agent evaluates material, temperature exposure, and intended use.

### Why the agent cannot decide this alone

The mesh does not contain reliable authorship, licensing, safety, assembly, or use-case information. An agent may extract clues, but it must not treat guesses as project facts.

### What should remain

- Project name and saved/unsaved state
- Project description
- Author and license
- Safety and usage instructions
- Reference pictures
- Assembly instructions
- Bill of materials and accessories
- Important profile notes
- Project save, version, backup, and ownership controls

### What the agent should do

The agent should read this material before planning the print, highlight contradictions, and ask about missing safety or assembly information when relevant.

Only the project name and saved/unsaved state need to remain in the normal Project-window chrome. The rest belongs in the Project details drawer and surfaces automatically only when consequential:

- Safety or usage warning: on import, when it affects planning, and before Print
- License restriction: when sharing, publishing, using commercially, or exporting
- Assembly instructions: for multi-part projects and plate organization
- Bill of materials or accessories: when non-printed components are required
- Reference image: when it clarifies orientation, color, or intended appearance
- Profile note: when the agent proposes deviating from it
- Recovery or version warning: when work is unsaved or versions conflict

The user should not have to open Project details for its contents to influence the plan.

---

## 2.2 Physical printer setup

This surface answers: **What hardware and material will actually perform the print?**

### What should remain

- Target printer
- Nozzle diameter and nozzle type
- Build-plate type
- Loaded filament and material
- Filament color
- AMS or multi-material slot mapping
- Printer availability and current condition
- Important mismatches between configuration and observed hardware

### Why the agent cannot decide this alone

Configured state and physical state can diverge. Selecting “PLA” in software does not establish that PLA is actually loaded, dry, correctly mapped, or compatible with the installed plate and nozzle.

### What the agent should do

- Discover printers and materials automatically
- Read AMS and printer state where available
- Compare observed state with the project
- Recommend compatible profiles
- Explain mismatches
- Ask the user only about unresolved physical facts

The existing setup wizard’s enormous lists of printer and filament profiles should become hardware discovery followed by a short confirmation.

---

## 2.3 Print intent

This surface answers: **What outcome does the user want?**

Instead of beginning with hundreds of process parameters, the product should ask for meaningful requirements.

### What should remain

- Intended use
- Visual versus functional priority
- Strength direction
- Accuracy requirements
- Important dimensions or clearances
- Heat, chemical, outdoor, food-contact, or flexibility requirements
- Desired surface quality
- Maximum acceptable print time
- Material or color requirements
- Acceptable and unacceptable support contact
- Whether this is a prototype or final part

### Why the agent cannot decide this alone

The same model can legitimately be printed with different orientations, materials, wall structures, infill, supports, and tolerances depending on its purpose.

A decorative prototype and a load-bearing final component may use identical geometry but require completely different plans.

### What the agent should do

Translate intent into technical settings. For example:

> “This is a visible decorative object, so I oriented it to protect the front surface, moved the seam to the rear, and accepted a longer print to reduce visible layer artifacts.”

The user should judge that reasoning without having to configure every underlying value.

The full intent editor should appear during project creation, import, or when requirements are incomplete. Afterward, Prepare should retain only a compact editable summary. Specialized questions such as food contact, flexibility, critical clearances, and protected support surfaces should appear contextually rather than in every project.

---

## 2.4 Objects, parts, and plates

This surface answers: **What exactly is included in this job?**

OrcaSlicer’s object and plate tree is essential, although its presentation can be simplified.

### What should remain

- Every plate in the project
- Every object and part
- Object names
- Quantity and duplicates
- Which objects are enabled
- Which material or extruder each object uses
- Modifiers, support enforcers, and support blockers
- Object-specific requirements
- Print order where it matters
- Search for complex projects

### Why the agent cannot decide this alone

The agent cannot assume that every imported object should be printed or that apparently duplicated parts are accidental. A modifier may encode engineering intent that is invisible in the rendered outer surface.

Multi-plate organization can also represent batches, material differences, alternative versions, or assembly groups.

### What the agent should do

Arrange objects, detect accidental overlaps, identify likely duplicates, balance plates, and suggest grouping—but show the resulting job manifest for confirmation.

For a simple one-object, one-material, one-plate project, show a compact job summary by default. Expand the full object-and-part tree contextually when the project contains multiple objects, parts, plates, materials, modifiers, or print-order constraints. Search should appear only when the project is complex enough to need it.

---

## 2.5 Essential geometry editing

This surface answers: **Does the printable geometry need to be intentionally changed?**

This was underrepresented in the previous report. Geometry editing must remain a first-class capability.

### Default operations

- Add and remove models
- Select parts
- Move, rotate, and scale
- Place a model on a chosen face
- Arrange models on the plate
- Duplicate and change quantity
- Undo and redo

### Contextual operations

These remain first-class capabilities but should appear under More, through the selected-object menu, or when the situation calls for them:

- Mirror
- Cut and split
- Merge or assemble related parts
- Add text or labels
- Measure dimensions and clearances
- Work with multiple plates
- Repair or identify problematic geometry
- Create intentional modifiers
- Paint supports, seams, materials, or other region-specific behavior

Examples of contextual surfacing include offering Cut for an oversized model, Measure when fit or clearance matters, Repair when mesh defects are detected, and region annotation when the agent cannot determine where support contact is acceptable.

### Why the agent cannot decide this alone

Changing geometry can change the object’s meaning.

The agent cannot safely assume that it may:

- Cut a model into pieces
- Fill or enlarge a hole
- Change scale
- Move two components relative to one another
- Mirror an asymmetric part
- Emboss text
- Remove an apparently unnecessary detail
- Reorient an assembly
- Create a different mating surface

Even when a change improves printability, it may make the part unusable.

### What the agent should do

The agent may propose geometry changes and generate previews:

> “Splitting the model here eliminates most supports and hides the joint on the rear surface.”

But the user should review meaning-changing operations. Direct manipulation must remain available because communicating spatial corrections in words is often slower than moving or painting them on the model.

---

## 2.6 Local meaning and region-level overrides

This surface answers: **Are different parts or surfaces subject to different requirements?**

Global instructions such as “make it strong” are often insufficient.

### What should remain

Users need ways to identify:

- Faces that must remain smooth
- Surfaces where support contact is allowed or forbidden
- Precision holes and mating surfaces
- Areas requiring additional strength
- Flexible or sacrificial regions
- Visible versus hidden faces
- Preferred or forbidden seam locations
- Different material or color regions
- Areas where texture is intentional
- Object-specific print requirements

### Why the agent cannot decide this alone

Computer vision can estimate geometry, but it cannot reliably know the functional role of every region.

For example, an agent may place a seam on the geometrically least visible face, unaware that the face mates with another part. It may strengthen the thickest region even though failure occurs around a small mounting hole.

### What the agent should do

Use semantic labels to generate modifiers and technical settings automatically. Users should describe meaning; they should not normally need to configure local speeds, wall counts, or infill percentages themselves.

---

## 2.7 Agent print plan

This surface answers: **What strategy has the agent chosen, and why?**

This is the AI-first replacement for most of OrcaSlicer’s process-setting panels.

### What should be shown by default

- Selected orientation
- Overall material, strength, support, and surface-quality strategy
- Most important assumption the agent could not verify
- Most important compromise or unresolved risk

### What should appear when expanded

- Detailed rationale and alternative plans
- Confidence by decision
- Important deviations from the normal printer profile
- Full change history
- Numerical implementation settings through the expert layer

### Why this surface is needed

Even when the agent has enough information to choose technical values, hiding its entire plan would make errors difficult to recognize.

The user may not need to know that a particular wall speed is 72 mm/s, but they should know that the plan emphasizes surface quality over speed.

### What the agent can normally control

- Layer-height strategy
- Line widths
- Wall and top/bottom structure
- Infill density and pattern
- Speeds and acceleration
- Cooling and temperature within qualified ranges
- Retraction and wiping
- Bridge behavior
- Support style, density, and interface parameters
- Brim, skirt, priming, and adhesion aids
- Purging and flushing calculations
- Seam implementation after the user states the preferred region
- Printer-specific G-code from a trusted profile

These settings should remain accessible to experts, but they do not need to be primary beginner-facing surfaces.

Do not always show time and material estimates in Prepare. Show them there only after a valid background slice exists. Until then, the plan can say `Ready to check`.

---

## 2.8 Check print: print-plan verification

This surface answers: **What will the printer actually do?**

OrcaSlicer’s Preview capability is not merely an expert visualization. It is the last opportunity to discover a bad plan before material and machine time are consumed. **Check print** opens the current valid slice in a modal window using Orca's real Preview widget and G-code renderer. The window closes if that slice or its project changes. For now, Print stays the primary action for every valid slice and Check print stays in its menu; agent findings do not change that action.

### Default verification

- Overall appearance of the sliced result
- Estimated time
- Material usage and cost
- Highest-priority warnings
- Comparison with the user’s stated intent

When supports exist, support verification becomes the default Check view:

- Support locations
- Contact surfaces and likely scars
- Supports that may be difficult to remove
- Supports entering holes, cavities, or mating regions
- A direct Adjust supports or Mark protected areas action that returns to Prepare

If no supports exist, Check should emphasize the most consequential detected risk instead.

### Contextual verification

- Seams on protected or visible surfaces
- Risky bridges and overhangs
- Thin or missing features
- First-layer contact problems
- Unsupported islands
- Unexpected gaps or collisions
- Material or color changes
- Purge volume and waste
- Prime tower and extruder assignments

### Expert verification

OrcaSlicer’s more detailed views should remain available on demand:

- Line type
- Layer height
- Line width
- Speed
- Fan speed
- Temperature
- Volumetric flow
- Layer time
- Extruder assignment
- Layer-by-layer playback
- Individual toolpath playback
- Visibility toggles for walls, infill, bridges, supports, travel, retraction, wiping, and seams
- Raw G-code inspection

### Why the agent cannot independently verify its own plan

The preview is produced from the same assumptions and algorithms that created the plan. It is evidence, but it is not independent knowledge of the user’s intent.

An agent may verify that a toolpath is internally consistent while still misunderstanding which surface must remain smooth or which opening must stay unobstructed.

### What the agent should do

Inspect the complete preview automatically and present a short risk-focused report. The user should review the meaningful consequences instead of manually examining every toolpath by default.

Layer count and the complete extrusion-role legend are not beginner decision aids. Keep them in Inspect toolpaths with the other expert diagnostics.

---

## 2.9 Print preflight

This surface answers: **Is the correct job about to be sent to the correct physical machine?**

Prepare should contain a visible Print entry point. Print opens this preflight; it does not bypass it:

`Print -> Send preflight -> explicit Send`

The current Print action opens Orca's existing Select Machine or printer-host send dialog, which requires a separate send/upload choice. The complete JusPrin preflight checklist below remains future product work.

### What should remain

- Job name and thumbnail
- Destination printer
- Selected plate
- Time and material estimate
- Filament and AMS mapping
- Plate-type confirmation
- Bed-leveling choice
- Flow-calibration choice
- Timelapse choice
- First-layer inspection
- Build-plate detection
- Tangle and clumping detection
- AI-monitoring behavior and sensitivity
- Recovery options
- Warnings about disabled checks
- Explicit Send control

### Why the agent cannot decide this alone

This is where digital assumptions become a real physical operation. The chosen printer may be occupied, prepared with another plate, located remotely, or loaded with valuable material.

Some monitoring options also involve privacy, camera use, false-positive tolerance, or printer-specific limitations.

### What the agent should do

Perform the preflight, recommend safe defaults, and block obviously inconsistent jobs. The user should see a concise checklist and authorize sending.

---

## 2.10 Live printing and device control

This surface answers: **What is happening now, and can the user intervene?**

OrcaSlicer’s Device surface demonstrates that an AI slicer is also partly a printer-control product.

### What should remain immediately accessible

- Camera
- Job progress
- Current layer and remaining time
- Printer state
- Nozzle and bed temperatures
- Important fan or light controls
- Health and fault alerts
- Pause
- Resume
- Stop

Manual movement, homing, detailed fan control, storage, and file management can be contextual or expert functions.

### Why the agent cannot control this invisibly

Sensors and vision systems can be wrong. Users may notice a sound, smell, obstruction, detaching part, or safety concern that the system cannot observe.

Pause and stop are human override mechanisms. They should never be hidden inside a conversation or require the agent’s cooperation.

### What the agent should do

Monitor the job, explain anomalies, recommend intervention, and automatically pause only under rules the user has authorized in advance. It should clearly report why an automatic intervention occurred.

---

## 2.11 Calibration and troubleshooting

This surface answers: **Is the printer-material combination behaving as expected?**

The audit found both guided calibration pages and more advanced generators.

### Relevant calibration capabilities

- Flow dynamics
- Flow rate
- Temperature
- Pressure advance
- Retraction
- Maximum volumetric speed
- VFA
- Junction deviation
- Input-shaping frequency and damping

### Why the agent cannot completely own calibration

Calibration depends on physical evidence:

- Filament may be wet.
- Adhesion may be poor.
- Transparent or reflective filament may confuse optical sensors.
- A nozzle may be worn or partially obstructed.
- A user may judge two samples differently.
- Automatic measurements contain uncertainty.
- An apparently better surface may reduce strength or accuracy elsewhere.

### What the agent should do

The agent should:

1. Diagnose the observed symptom.
2. Decide whether calibration is justified.
3. Select the appropriate test.
4. Choose safe test ranges.
5. Explain what to observe.
6. Analyze sensor data or photographs.
7. Recommend a result.
8. Ask the user to confirm before updating a persistent printer or filament profile.

The user should not be presented with every calibration parameter unless manual control is requested.

---

## 2.12 Privacy, updates, portability, and expert administration

These functions are used less frequently, but they are important for particular users and organizations.

### User-owned decisions

- Cloud login region
- Stealth or offline mode
- Network-plugin use
- Preset synchronization
- Multi-device management
- Firmware and application update timing
- Camera and monitoring privacy
- Backup and recovery policy
- Importing and replacing configurations
- Ownership and export of project data

### Capabilities that should remain available

- Import 3MF, STL, STEP, SVG, OBJ, AMF, ZIP archives, and configurations
- Export models, projects, sliced plates, G-code, and preset bundles
- Export printer, filament, and process profiles
- Manage downloaded and stored printer files
- Access timelapses
- Run network diagnostics
- Open configuration data
- Enable developer tools

### Why the agent cannot decide these alone

These choices affect privacy, compatibility, organizational policy, intellectual property, and the user’s ability to leave the product.

The agent can simplify the workflows, but it should not silently enable cloud communication, install firmware, replace profiles, or trap projects in a proprietary format.

---

# 3. Recommended final product structure

The application should use one main window rather than turning every stage of a print into equal global navigation.

## 3.1 Home

Home is the hub for:

- Printer cards showing availability, condition, and loaded filament
- Project gallery, open, and project status
- Import of 3MF, STL, STEP, SVG, OBJ, AMF, and ZIP files
- Entry to project versions and backups
- Launching Monitor

## 3.2 Project window

The Project window contains the print-planning lifecycle without dividing it into equal destinations:

- **Prepare:** dominant workspace containing intent, objects and plates, the 3D canvas, geometry editing, local meaning, and the agent plan
- **Check print:** temporary sliced-verification mode
- **Project details:** drawer for authoritative project knowledge
- **Print:** entry point to Send preflight

Prepare may point to Printer Configuration, but it does not own machine calibration, filament inventory, maintenance, or privacy settings.

## 3.3 Printer Configuration

Printer Configuration owns:

- Target printer, nozzle, and build-plate configuration
- Loaded filament, material colors, AMS, and multi-material inventory
- Calibration workflows
- Troubleshooting and maintenance
- Firmware-update timing
- Camera and monitoring privacy
- Network plugins and diagnostic tools
- Stored printer files and timelapses

Prepare displays a compact pointer to this state and surfaces mismatches; it does not duplicate the complete configuration UI.

## 3.4 Monitor

Monitor is a pop-out surface so it can remain visible while the user works elsewhere. It owns:

- Camera
- Progress, current layer, and remaining time
- Printer state
- Nozzle and bed temperatures
- Health and fault alerts
- Pause, Resume, and Stop as never-hidden human overrides

Manual movement, homing, detailed fan or light control, storage, and file management are contextual.

## 3.5 Overlays and application-level layers

- **Send preflight:** final job, destination, material mapping, safety, and monitoring confirmation followed by explicit Send
- **Expert layer:** raw process settings, numeric per-object and per-region overrides, manual calibration ranges, toolpath diagnostics, and G-code
- **Preferences:** cloud region, stealth/offline behavior, network plugins, sync, updates, privacy, backup and recovery, import/export administration, and developer tools

This structure preserves the lifecycle of a print without turning Setup, Intent, Plan, Verify, Print, Monitor, and Diagnose into nine equal screens.

---

# 4. Visibility hierarchy

## 4.1 Default

Continuously visible in the ordinary Project window:

- Project name and saved/unsaved state
- Current printer, nozzle, plate, and material summary
- Compact intent summary
- Compact active plate and object summary
- 3D Prepare canvas
- Add, remove, select, move, rotate, scale, place on face, arrange, duplicate, Undo, and Redo
- Compact agent plan
- Highest unresolved assumption or risk
- Check print and Print

Inside Check, the default changes to sliced appearance, time, material, cost, the highest-priority warning, and comparison with intent. When supports exist, support placement and removal risk become the default Check emphasis.

## 4.2 Contextual

Shown when the project or current task makes it relevant:

- Full object, part, and plate tree
- Per-object material or extruder
- Modifiers, support enforcers, blockers, print order, and search
- Local surface annotations and object-specific requirements
- Mirror, cut, split, merge, assemble, text, measure, repair, positive/negative parts, and multi-plate distribution
- Seam, bridge, overhang, thin-feature, first-layer, island, and collision inspection
- Material changes, purge waste, prime tower, and extruder assignments
- Time and material estimate in Prepare after a valid background slice exists
- Assembly instructions, accessories, and reference pictures
- Calibration and maintenance recommendations
- Firmware updates, storage, timelapses, and multi-device management

## 4.3 On demand

Available through Project details, More, or the expert layer:

- Full intent questionnaire after it has been completed
- Project description, author, license, pictures, BOM, assembly guide, and profile notes
- Version, backup, ownership, and export administration
- Detailed agent rationale, alternatives, confidence, profile deviations, and change history
- Individual speeds and accelerations
- Exact line widths
- Infill and support implementation parameters
- Retraction, wiping, cooling, and purge details
- Complete toolpath legend and playback
- Raw G-code
- Manual calibration ranges
- Network tests, configuration folders, developer mode, and visualization preferences

## 4.4 Interruptive

Normally hidden, but presented prominently at the point where the user can resolve it:

- Wrong printer, nozzle, plate, or filament
- Safety or usage instruction relevant to the current plan
- Unsupported, missing, or defective geometry
- Support entering a protected region
- Violated dimensional requirement
- Material incompatible with the stated use
- Agent uncertainty about a meaning-changing geometry operation
- License conflict during sharing, publishing, commercial use, or export
- Unsaved work, recovery issue, or version conflict
- Printer-health or safety alert

---

# 5. The final design rule

For every OrcaSlicer control, ask four questions:

1. **Does this require physical information the software may not possess?**
   Keep a user confirmation surface.

2. **Does this depend on the object’s purpose, meaning, or the user’s taste?**
   Keep an intent, annotation, or direct-editing surface.

3. **Does this authorize a consequential, legal, private, or physical action?**
   Keep explicit user control.

4. **Is this merely a technical method for achieving an already-understood goal?**
   Let the agent manage it and expose it only when explanation or expert control is needed.

That rule preserves the genuinely human parts of OrcaSlicer while allowing the agent to remove most of its parameter complexity.

1	# JusPrin design system
2	
3	**Status:** Canonical product and brand guidance for `jusprin-newui`.
4	
5	JusPrin should make advanced 3D printing feel immediate: a confident path from model to machine that removes detours without hiding control. The product should feel focused, assured, inventive, and approachable. Its voice is direct, capable, and optimistic—never cute, cryptic, or over-engineered.
6	
7	The original JusPrin logo was supplied by the user and restored from repository revision `6eecb78b19`. The purple gradient endpoints were verified from the source SVG. Positioning language in the POC brand kit is proposed product direction, not an externally sourced market claim.
8	
9	## Brand behavior
10	
11	- **Focused:** every element earns its place.
12	- **Assured:** guidance is calm and actions are decisive.
13	- **Inventive:** the product is technical without being intimidating.
14	- **Approachable:** use plain language instead of slicer jargon where possible.
15	- Make the next action obvious. Brand behavior should feel as focused as the visual system.
16	
17	The logo suggests an end-to-end journey through its orbit, precision and momentum through the crossing diagonals, flexible control through the open circle, and technical confidence softened by warmth through the purple gradient.
18	
19	Write the name exactly as **JusPrin**: capital J and P, no space, never all caps in body copy. Use surrounding text color for the name in ordinary copy; do not force a gradient into small text.

22	
23	The primary expressions are the horizontal lockup, the compact product mark, and the text wordmark. Use the compact mark for application icons and small product contexts.
24	
25	- Clear space: at least one quarter of the mark width on every side.
26	- Minimum digital mark: 24 px.
27	- Minimum digital horizontal lockup: 120 px.
28	- Minimum printed mark: 8 mm.
29	- Minimum printed lockup: 32 mm.
30	- Below these sizes, use the mark alone and verify that the orbit arcs remain distinct.

32	Always use the original artwork, preserve its aspect ratio and components, maintain clear space, and place it on White, Mist, Ink, or another quiet solid field. Do not stretch, rotate, redraw, arbitrarily recolor, outline, shadow, separate, or place it directly over visual noise. Monochrome is allowed only when required. If the center crossing or orbit loses clarity, increase size, contrast, or space.

159	## Writing UI code
160	
161	Rules for anyone, human or agent, adding or changing a JusPrin surface. They
162	exist because every value that is typed by hand drifts from Figma and from
163	the other side of the app within weeks; today's guards catch most of it, but
164	only if the code goes through the token file in the first place.
165	
166	1. **Never type a color, radius, font, or control size.** Every one comes
167	   from `resources/jusprin/ui/design-tokens.json`. Native code reads it
168	   through `ShellTheme`: `palette(dark)` for color, `metrics()` for radii,
169	   spacing, and per-component sizes, `font(role)` for type. A stock
170	   `wxStaticText`, `wxTextCtrl`, or OrcaSlicer `Button` is
171	   dressed through `Shell/ShellRecipes.hpp`, never by calling its setters
172	   with literals. The Agent page uses only `var(--…)`: `--<group>-<name>` for
173	   color, `--radius-<name>`, `--font-<role>`, `--font-code`, and
174	   `--button-<recipe>-padding`.
175	2. **If the value you need has no token, add the token first.** Put it in
176	   the JSON, extend the guard in `tests/brand/test_brand_tokens.cpp` so a
177	   later edit cannot silently move it, then read it from code. Do not write
178	   the number "for now": the guards cannot see a literal that is already
179	   there, and the next reader cannot tell a decision from an accident. A
180	   value that exists in Figma but not in the roles or scales is a design
181	   decision to raise, not a reason to type it.
182	3. **Layout spacing may stay literal, on the scale.** Padding between
183	   regions, gaps, and margins use 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 32, 40, or 48 DIP.
184	   Control padding is not layout spacing; it comes from a button recipe.
185	4. **Pick the nearest role, never a bespoke size.** The roles are the whole
186	   type system. Bold at a body or label size is a role of its own; if a
187	   surface seems to need a size that no role has, see rule 2.
188	5. **Read the code on `jusprin-newui`, not old commit messages or Figma,
189	   when they disagree.** The header's chip and menu dimensions were once
190	   changed to match Figma and reverted because they looked worse; the
191	   token file records what stayed.
192	6. **Run the guards before calling UI work done:** `brand_tokens_tests`,
193	   `shell_theme_tests`, and `npm test` in `AgentUI`. Then look at the surface
194	   in the running app; the guards prove the code went through the tokens,
195	   not that the result looks right.
196	7. **Upstream files are off limits for style.** OrcaSlicer's own screens are
197	   retinted through the hooks `BrandPalette.cpp` installs and nothing else;
198	   see [Fork stewardship](fork-stewardship.md). Their radii and fonts stay
199	   OrcaSlicer's until the surface is replaced.
200	
201	## Runtime application in the native app
202	
203	The token file is applied to the running application in three layers. All
204	three read `resources/jusprin/ui/design-tokens.json`; none of them carries a
205	color literal of its own, and the whole layer touches OrcaSlicer code in only
206	three small, additive seams plus one attachment point.
207	
208	1. **Fork-owned surfaces** (`src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Shell/*`, the React Agent
209	   page) resolve every style through the token file, not only color.
210	   - Native: `ShellTheme` exposes `palette(dark)` for color, `metrics()` for
211	     the radius and spacing scales and the per-component sizes, `font(role)`
212	     for the type roles above. It is loaded once, by `Brand/BrandPalette.cpp`, and passed
213	     by reference into every shell widget. Widgets that paint themselves read
214	     it directly; a stock `wxStaticText`, `wxTextCtrl`, or OrcaSlicer `Button`
215	     is dressed through the three functions in `Shell/ShellRecipes.hpp`, so no
216	     fork-owned C++ file names an OrcaSlicer font preset or writes a radius as
217	     a number. `tests/jusprin/test_shell_theme.cpp` checks the parse and the
218	     fonts.
219	   - Web: `AgentUI/src/tokens.ts` writes the semantic colors as
220	     `--<group>-<name>` on every appearance change, and once at startup the
221	     radii as `--radius-<name>` and each type role as a complete `font`
222	     shorthand, `--font-<role>` in the UI face, plus `--font-code` for the one
223	     monospace role. The stylesheet may only say `var(--…)` for color, radius,
224	     and type; `AgentUI/src/styles.test.ts` reads the stylesheet from disk and
225	     fails on any literal, and on any spacing value off the scale.
226	   - Canvas: the Prepare canvas's tool strip (`Canvas/ViewportToolStrip`)
227	     paints with ImGui inside the GL frame, from the same `ShellTheme`. Its
228	     icons are the `currentColor` SVGs in `resources/jusprin/ui/icons`,
229	     rasterized white and tinted with the token colour. ImGui 1.83 has no
230	     shadow primitive, so `elevation.medium` is approximated with stacked
231	     translucent rounded rectangles.
232	2. **Retained OrcaSlicer surfaces** are retinted through the color tables
233	   OrcaSlicer already routes its colors through, installed once per appearance
234	   mode by `JusPrin/Brand/BrandPalette.cpp` from the end of
235	   `GUI_App::init_label_colours`:
236	   - `StateColor::SetColorOverrides` maps OrcaSlicer's brand and surface
237	     literals (teal family, grays, whites, text grays) to semantic tokens before
